paper_metadata.title: Evaluation of quantum algorithms for pricing and computation of VaR (D5.4)

summary: The report evaluates quantum accelerated Monte Carlo for derivative pricing and VaR using amplitude estimation variants (CQPEAE, IQPEAE, IQAE, MLAE) and introduces a new encoding plus the Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm. Simulations on discretized Black–Scholes models (5 qubits, 32 intervals) show the expected quadratic convergence scaling (error ∝ 1/C vs classical 1/√C) and demonstrate that the new encoding and RQAE can handle negative payoffs, but all results are obtained on noiseless simulators (QLM/FT3) with no practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Standard-encoding quantum accelerated Monte Carlo pricing experiments for European call, European put, digital call, digital put, and futures payoffs using four gate-based amplitude-estimation variants.

algorithm.variant: QAMC pricing with standard encoding; AE variants CQPEAE, IQPEAE, IQAE, MLAE
algorithm.optimizer: MLAE uses a brute optimizer from scipy.optimize if no custom optimizer is provided; others not specified

optimizer_settings.optimizer: brute optimizer from scipy.optimize (MLAE only, if no custom optimizer provided)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Standard encoding loads the probability distribution with load_probability and the payoff with load_array; the encoded amplitude is proportional to sqrt(p(xi)V(xi)) and the final measured probability estimates the Riemann sum via AE.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[V(ST)|Ft] for option payoffs under Black-Scholes dynamics via Monte Carlo/QAMC; equivalently approximate sum_i p(x_i)V(x_i).

problem_instance.description: Pricing of European call, European put, digital call, digital put, and futures under a Black-Scholes underlying.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Black-Scholes probability distribution discretized on [0.01, 5.0] with 5 qubits / 32 intervals; payoffs loaded into quantum circuit amplitudes.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulations repeated per configuration; 10 repetitions for CQPEAE, IQAE, MLAE and 5 for IQPEAE. Error measured as absolute difference between QAMC estimate and Riemann sum across increasing oracle calls.

hardware.device_name: QLM simulator and FT3 HPC node

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical Monte Carlo / Euler-Maruyama and Riemann-sum reference values used for comparison; option pricing problem setup from Black-Scholes parameters.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Absolute error versus Riemann sum; convergence plots over number of oracle calls.

speedup_claims.conditions: in the ideal QAMC setting; Table 1 states O(1/sqrt(C)) for CMC vs O(1/C) for QAMC in d dimensions
speedup_claims.caveats: The report states the quantum advantage is not achievable on current hardware; deep AE circuits and large qubit requirements limit practicality.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/C) for QAMC in d dimensions (as stated in Table 1); standard Monte Carlo baseline O(1/sqrt(C))

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not estimated in the report; theoretical scaling advantage only (O(1/C) vs O(1/sqrt(C))).
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires large fault‑tolerant circuits implementing amplitude estimation with deep Grover-like routines and efficient SDE simulation; authors explicitly state current NISQ devices cannot run these circuits.
limiting_factors: Oracle construction for SDE simulation requires very large qubit counts
Deep amplitude-estimation circuits incompatible with NISQ coherence times
Quantum gates currently slower than classical Monte Carlo operations
Efficient data loading of probability distributions is costly

notes: Hardware is reported as QLM and FT3 in Tables 6 and 7; QLM treated as simulator_other.

No total qubit count is explicitly given for the full standard-encoding experiments; 5-qubit domain discretization is reported, but the full circuit also includes ancilla/registers, so num_qubits left null and not inferred.
Circuit depth is not explicitly quantified; only qualitative statements about deep circuits and AE routines are given.
Section 4 explicitly states the quantum algorithm is 'not competitive yet with respect to classical algorithms when executed on NISQ architectures'.
Speedup discussed only as theoretical quadratic scaling improvement.

experiments.description: New-encoding quantum accelerated Monte Carlo pricing experiments for the same option set, adding the Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm and comparing against CQPEAE, IQPEAE, IQAE, and MLAE.

algorithm.variant: QAMC pricing with new encoding; AE variants CQPEAE, IQPEAE, IQAE, MLAE, and RQAE
algorithm.optimizer: RQAE and other AE methods use their respective internal procedures; MLAE uses brute optimizer from scipy.optimize if no custom optimizer is provided

optimizer_settings.optimizer: brute optimizer from scipy.optimize (MLAE only, if no custom optimizer provided)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: New encoding loads probability distribution and payoff directly (not square roots), using an extra qubit; after Hadamard transforms the measured amplitude is proportional to the signed Riemann sum.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[V(ST)|Ft] for option payoffs under Black-Scholes dynamics via QAMC; for new encoding, the amplitude encodes (1/2^n) sum_i p(x_i)V(x_i).

problem_instance.description: Pricing of European call, European put, digital call, digital put, and futures under a Black-Scholes underlying, including a negative-payoff futures case and a negative-value payoff example with K=1.5S0.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Black-Scholes probability distribution discretized on [0.01, 5.0] with 5 qubits / 32 intervals; new encoding uses direct loading of probability and payoff values.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulations repeated per configuration; 10 repetitions for CQPEAE, IQAE, MLAE and 5 for IQPEAE, 100 for IQAE and RQAE in Table 7. Error measured as absolute difference between QAMC estimate and Riemann sum across increasing oracle calls.

hardware.device_name: QLM simulator and FT3 HPC node

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical Monte Carlo / Euler-Maruyama and Riemann-sum reference values used for comparison; option pricing problem setup from Black-Scholes parameters.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Absolute error versus Riemann sum; convergence plots over number of oracle calls; comparison of RQAE against other AE methods.

speedup_claims.conditions: QAMC with new encoding and AE; report states the same asymptotic O(1/C) vs O(1/sqrt(C)) comparison as the standard encoding case
speedup_claims.caveats: New encoding introduces a factor Npaths in the amplitude relation, which can overshadow or eliminate practical speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/C) for QAMC in d dimensions (as stated in Table 1); standard Monte Carlo baseline O(1/sqrt(C))

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not provided; constant factor Npaths in Eq. (3.9) may eliminate practical speedup.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Large-scale fault‑tolerant hardware capable of implementing deep amplitude-estimation circuits and efficient oracle preparation for stochastic simulations.
limiting_factors: Large constant factor Npaths reduces practical advantage
High qubit requirements for SDE simulation
All experiments performed in noiseless simulation only

notes: Hardware is reported as QLM and FT3 in Table 7; QLM treated as simulator_other.
The new encoding requires one additional qubit, but the full circuit qubit count is not explicitly stated; num_qubits left null.
Circuit depth is discussed qualitatively (RQAE allows shallower circuits for larger q) but no numeric depth is reported.
Section 3.1 and Section 4 acknowledge that the Npaths factor can 'overshadow or even kill the speedup'.
Experiments only benchmark convergence behaviour in simulation.
